rows.label: Typical-year hourly weather and solar, central London (51.507, −0.128)

source.title: PVGIS v5.3 typical meteorological year (European Commission Joint Research Centre)

rows.rationale: Fetched at build time by scripts/fetch-pvgis.ts and trimmed to four columns: T2m (air temperature, °C), G(h) (global horizontal), Gb(n) (beam normal) and Gd(h) (diffuse horizontal) irradiance in W/m². Timestamps are UTC, as PVGIS gives them; there are 8,760 hours with no leap day. Each month comes from a different source year, listed in the snapshot's monthsSelected.

rows.label: Offset added to every hourly outdoor temperature
rows.rationale: Zero for the typical year. Tests set it below zero to build a colder year and check that heat demand rises.

rows.label: Minutes past the hour at which the snapshot's irradiance values apply
rows.rationale: The engine places the sun at this time within each UTC hour when it splits irradiance onto walls. The PVGIS typical year labels each hour HH:00. The 10 minutes is inferred from the data, not from PVGIS documentation: checked on the snapshot on 18 October 2026: global horizontal should equal beam normal × cos(zenith) + diffuse horizontal, and the mean absolute mismatch, as a share of annual global irradiance, is 1.5% with the sun at HH:00, 0.24% at HH:10 and 2.6% at HH:30. A test repeats this check.

rows.label: Total floor area
rows.rationale: The phase 1 archetype is a two-storey 1930–49 semi of about 90 m²: two storeys of 45 m². Not overridable yet: heated volume and the wall, roof and floor areas are stored from this value, so an override would not flow through to them. Phase 3 decides how overrides work.

rows.label: Storey height (used for wall height and heated volume)
rows.rationale: Typical room height for the period. RdSAP 10 adds a floor void between storeys; that is ignored here, which slightly understates wall area and volume.

rows.label: Heated volume
rows.rationale: Total floor area × storey height: 90 × 2.5.

rows.label: Exposed perimeter of the footprint (walls and ground floor)
rows.rationale: A 45 m² footprint of about 6.5 m × 7 m: front, back and one side wall. The party wall is excluded. Used for the external wall area and for the ground floor's perimeter-to-area ratio.

rows.label: Window area

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: RdSAP window-area formula for houses in age bands A–C: 0.122 × floor area + 6.875 = 17.855 m². Split equally across north, east, south and west for solar gains. Not overridable yet: the net wall area is stored net of this value, so an override would not flow through to it. Phase 3 decides how overrides work.

rows.label: External door area

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: RdSAP standard area for one external door.

rows.label: Net external wall area
rows.rationale: Exposed perimeter × storey height × 2 storeys, less window and door area: 20 × 2.5 × 2 − 17.855 − 1.85 = 80.295 m².

rows.label: Roof (loft floor) area
rows.rationale: The loft floor equals the footprint: half the total floor area of a two-storey house.

rows.label: Ground floor area
rows.rationale: Equals the footprint: half the total floor area of a two-storey house.

rows.label: External wall U-value (unfilled cavity)

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: England default for an unfilled cavity wall in age bands A–E. Fabric uncertainty is carried by fabric.qualityFactor, not by this row.
rows.overrideHint: Lower if your cavity walls have been filled.

rows.label: Party wall U-value

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: The party wall of a 1930s semi is typically solid brick. SAP and RdSAP treat a solid party wall as having no heat loss (U = 0); an unfilled, unsealed cavity party wall would be 0.5. Convention to verify against the RdSAP 10 tables. The party wall area is therefore not needed.

rows.label: Window U-value (retrofitted double glazing)
rows.rationale: Retrofitted PVC double glazing of unknown date. RdSAP gives about 3.1 for glazing installed before 2002 and about 2.0 after; 2.8 leans to the older stock.
rows.overrideHint: About 2.0 for double glazing fitted since 2002, 1.4 or less for modern A-rated windows.

rows.label: External door U-value

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: RdSAP default for an external door.

rows.label: Roof U-value, main case (100 mm loft insulation)

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: RdSAP value for 100 mm of insulation at the joists. Magnus chose 100 mm as the main case on 17 October 2026, because most real 1930s semis have had loft insulation added.
rows.overrideHint: About 0.16 for 270 mm of loft insulation.

rows.label: Roof U-value, variant with no loft insulation

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: RdSAP default for a pitched roof in age bands A–D when loft insulation is unknown (treated as none). Kept for comparison with the main case; the calibration uses the main case.

rows.label: Ground floor U-value (uninsulated suspended timber)
rows.rationale: Uninsulated suspended timber floor. The exposed perimeter ÷ floor area ratio is 20 ÷ 45 ≈ 0.44, which gives about 0.75 W/m²K; the benchmark used the same 0.75. RdSAP computes this with the BS EN ISO 13370 method; that working is still to be done and recorded here, and may lower the value (the calibrated temperature absorbs the difference meanwhile).

rows.label: Air change rate (infiltration and ventilation)
rows.rationale: Older house with a suspended floor, an open or blocked chimney and some draughtproofing. SAP-style infiltration for this type is about 0.8–1.2. HEM, given an equivalent air permeability, worked out at about 0.89 over the year.

rows.label: Fabric quality factor (one multiplier on every U-value and the air change rate)

source.title: In-situ measurements of wall U-values in English housing (BRE for DECC, 2015)

rows.rationale: One shared factor, so independent draws of each U-value cannot average out and narrow the band. BRE found RdSAP's old solid-wall default was pessimistic by about a quarter, so the range reaches down to 0.75 (stock better than the tables) and up to 1.15 (worse, for example from poor workmanship). The mode is 1.0, the tables as given.

rows.label: Internal gains (occupants, lighting, appliances, cooking), constant
rows.rationale: SAP-style sum for about 2.5 occupants in 90 m²: metabolic, lighting, appliances, cooking and water heating, less evaporation losses, about 450 W. The range covers smaller and larger households and more or less efficient appliances. Constant all year; the max(0, …) clamp stops surplus summer gains producing negative demand.

rows.label: Window solar transmittance (g-value)

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: Total solar energy transmittance at normal incidence for double glazing, as used in the benchmark and the HEM input. To verify against the RdSAP 10 glazing table, including whether SAP's 0.9 factor for non-normal incidence applies on top.

rows.label: Window frame factor (glazed share of the window area)

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: SAP's frame factor for PVC-U frames. The HEM input uses the matching frame fraction of 0.3.

rows.label: Solar access (overshading) factor for windows

source.title: RdSAP 10 specification (BRE, June 2025)

rows.rationale: SAP's heating-season solar access factor for average overshading, the RdSAP default for a suburban street.

rows.label: Ground reflectance (albedo) seen by the walls
rows.rationale: The conventional value for snow-free ground in the isotropic-sky model, which the engine uses to put irradiance on the walls. A wall sees half the ground, so it receives 0.1 × global horizontal irradiance by reflection. Grass and paving range from about 0.1 to 0.3.

rows.label: Mean internal air temperature, heated continuously (calibrated to measured gas use)

source.title: DESNZ National Energy Efficiency Data-Framework (NEED) 2026 consumption data tables

rows.rationale: An air temperature, not an operative one. Calibrated so the archetype's central annual gas use (space heat plus hot water, divided by heating.boilerSeasonalEfficiency, with hot water from the hotWater rows and no cylinder loss for the combi) is 13,200 kWh, the midpoint of NEED's readings for comparable homes; the result must stay within their 10,980–15,433 kWh range. The target was fixed on 17 October 2026, before the engine existed. 15.7 °C solves that target with the hourly engine on the PVGIS typical year, with every other row at its default (npm run calibrate; solved 15.74 °C on 18 October 2026, rounded to 0.1 °C). The low and high (14.5 and 16.8 °C) are the temperatures that reproduce NEED's readings A (10,980 kWh) and C (15,433 kWh) by the same method: they describe uncertainty about the typical home, not the spread between households. The calibration may absorb fabric error from pessimistic RdSAP U-values as well as heating behaviour. It comes from gas-heated homes and applies to both setups, gas and heat pump ('the same household, different kit'); heat pump households often heat for longer, which biases the heat pump's running cost low.
rows.overrideHint: Lower if you heat only some rooms or only part of the day; higher if you keep the whole house warm all day.

rows.label: Gas combi boiler seasonal efficiency (space heat and hot water)
rows.rationale: Typical in-use seasonal efficiency of a condensing gas combi boiler serving a 1930s house. Condensing boilers rarely reach their rated 89–92% at radiator flow temperatures of 60–70 °C. Low 0.80 for a poorly set-up or older boiler; high 0.89 for a well-set-up boiler at lower flow temperatures. One efficiency covers both space heat and hot water. Gas is on a gross calorific value basis, as billed.
rows.overrideHint: Your boiler's seasonal efficiency, if known (for example from the Product Characteristics Database).

rows.label: Air source heat pump seasonal performance factor (space heat and hot water combined)

source.title: Energy Systems Catapult: Electrification of Heat interim heat pump performance data analysis report (2023)

rows.rationale: Fitted to field data. The Electrification of Heat trial's median air source SPF is 2.8; RHI monitoring found about 30% of air source heat pumps at 3.0 or above and about 8% at 3.5. A lognormal with median 2.8 and sigma 0.145 gives about 32% above 3.0 and 6% above 3.5, clipped to 2.0–4.0. The EoH figure is a whole-system SPF that includes hot water, so one SPF covers both uses and no separate hot water efficiency row is added; the exact system boundary (H2 or H4) is to verify. HeatpumpMonitor's figure of about 4.0 is a self-selected sample, kept for phase 2's 'well-installed' option rather than this range.
rows.overrideHint: Your heat pump's measured SPF, for example from its monitoring app over a full year.

rows.label: Hot water use
rows.rationale: About 100 litres a day for 2.5 occupants at the delivery temperature, close to SAP's 25 × occupants + 36 ≈ 98 litres. The range covers lighter and heavier users. With the delivery and cold-feed rows this is 100 × 4.18 × 40 ÷ 3600 ≈ 4.6 kWh of heat a day, about 1,700 kWh a year.
rows.overrideHint: More for more people or long showers; less for a smaller household.

rows.label: Hot water delivery temperature
rows.rationale: A typical tap and shower delivery temperature from a combi boiler or a heat pump cylinder.

rows.label: Cold water feed temperature (annual average)
rows.rationale: Annual average mains temperature in southern England. Monthly variation is phase 2.

rows.label: Hot water cylinder standing loss (heat pump setup only)
rows.rationale: A typical declared standing loss for a 200-litre factory-insulated heat pump cylinder; manufacturers' figures are about 1.2–1.9 kWh a day. The gas setup is a combi boiler and has no cylinder.
rows.overrideHint: The declared heat loss on your cylinder's label.

rows.label: Electricity unit rate, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Electricity carries no VAT from October 2026 to March 2027.
rows.overrideHint: The unit rate on your electricity bill.

rows.label: Electricity standing charge, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Paid by both setups.
rows.overrideHint: The standing charge on your electricity bill.

rows.label: Gas unit rate, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Includes 5% VAT. Per kWh on a gross calorific value basis, as billed.
rows.overrideHint: The unit rate on your gas bill.

rows.label: Gas standing charge, price cap, GB average, Direct Debit, 1 October–31 December 2026

source.title: Ofgem: Energy price cap unit rates and standing charges

rows.rationale: Includes 5% VAT. Paid only by the gas setup: the heat-pump-only house is assumed to have no gas hob and no gas supply.
rows.overrideHint: The standing charge on your gas bill.

rows.label: Natural gas carbon factor, gross calorific value (DESNZ 2026 factor set)

source.title: DESNZ: Greenhouse gas reporting: conversion factors 2026

rows.rationale: Scope 1 combustion factor for natural gas per kWh on a gross CV basis, which matches billed gas. The value is the recent editions' figure: DESNZ's 2026 summaries say fuel factors are mostly unchanged, but the exact 2026 cell in the full-set spreadsheet still needs checking. Well-to-tank emissions are excluded, as for electricity.

rows.label: Grid electricity carbon factor, annual average, electricity consumed (DESNZ 2026 factor set, 2025 data year)

source.title: DESNZ: 2026 GHG conversion factors methodology paper, Table 9 (including imported electricity)

rows.rationale: Electricity consumed, which includes transmission and distribution losses: 0.13096 for generation plus 0.01299 for losses, given as 0.14396 in Table 9. Well-to-tank emissions are excluded. An annual average; the hourly grid profile is phase 2.

rows.label: Base electricity use (lights and appliances), the same in both setups

source.title: Ofgem: Review of typical domestic consumption values, decision (May 2026), Table 1

rows.rationale: Ofgem's 2026 typical consumption values for single-rate electricity meters: low 1,600, medium 2,500 and high 3,800 kWh a year, used as the low, mode and high. Unlike most ranges here, this one is the spread between households, not uncertainty about a typical home: it is kept because base use is the same in both setups and cancels out of the paired difference, but it widens each setup's own cost band. Checked against Table 1 of the decision on 17 October 2026. A gas-heated home on a single-rate meter is the typical case these values describe. The boiler's own pump and fan electricity is left out in phase 1.
rows.overrideHint: Your annual electricity use from your bills, less any electric heating or car charging.
